validation.notes: Repaired all three modules of the recovery authorization-to-effect chain. (1) execution/effect-gate.ts: Gate.admit now runs the gate-state check before invoking the callback, so an aborting pass throws AbortRequested(cancellation) and a closed pass throws its close error synchronously instead of admitting the effect. (2) execution/tools.ts: executeToolCall passes the cleared/persisted call.args to tool.execute instead of the original toolCall.arguments, keeping identity fields from toolCall. (3) runtime/drive/tools.ts: recoverToolInvocation replays only when !cancelled, the tool still exists, the durable call declaration is 'safe' AND the tool declaration is 'safe' (was an || and no tool-existence check), so the old checkpoint is cleared and persisted arguments are used before invocation, while unsafe declarations, missing tools, cancellation, aborting/closed gates keep the conservative path they already had: read the checkpoint snapshot and publish an interruption outcome. Publication remains the last lifecycle step because performToolInvocation seals then drains the progress channel and pending live update delivery before resolving, and publishToolOutcome runs after it. Validation ran from the workspace root with no dependencies, network or credentials; output 'regression: OK', exit 0. The script exercises real modules via .prale-eval/subject.mjs with only checkpoint storage, the publication sink and the progress transport faked, and asserts cross-boundary behavior: gate admit rejection for aborting/closed states; executor receives cleared args rather than model args; event order clear -> invoke -> update -> checkpoint -> effect-complete -> seal -> drain -> drain-complete -> publish with a single publication that neither the effect nor the drain can observe; unsafe persisted declaration, unsafe tool declaration and a missing tool never invoke the effect and retain the checkpoint snapshot and interruption marker; cancelled, aborting-gate and closed-gate recovery never cross the effect boundary. Asynchronous ordering is controlled with promises only (no timers, randomness or external IO) and the script creates no input files. Mutation check: restoring each production file alone to its faulty baseline makes the script fail with an AssertionError for that file (gate: no AbortRequested thrown; executor: model arguments observed; drive: effect ran for an unsafe replay declaration); the fixed tree passes again afterwards. Optional limitation: no TypeScript compiler is installed in the workspace (node_modules/.bin/tsc absent) and installing dependencies was out of scope, so no separate tsc type-check was run; the required Node 24 vm-modules regression, which strips types from every loaded module, is the validation evidence.
